5	source of truth lives here, and [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## File reads: read the slice you need
13	
14	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs. Grep or read
15	further on demand.
16	
17	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
18	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
19	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`. Read further only when chasing a
20	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
21	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
22	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item, and grep to locate it first.
23	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small, so read it whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
24	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
25	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
26	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
27	  need.
28	
29	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
30	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline. The same "slice you need" rule applies
31	to historical files.
32	
33	## Notes references
34	
35	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
36	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
37	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
38	single-bracketed.
39	
40	## Reference numbering
41	
42	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
43	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
44	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
45	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
46	
47	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
48	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
49	file's number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
50	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
51	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
52	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation, so it needs no definition here. To
53	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
54	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
55	
56	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
57	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
58	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
59	as-built ladder, or a **same-file fragment**, `[N]: #<slug>`, a ladder rung's link to its own
60	subsection. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
61	exact shape.
62	
63	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
64	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md` is `## Todo`
65	then `## Done`, `chores-NN.md` top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
66	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
67	definitions move. Every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
68	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
69	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule. `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
70	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate, while `chores-NN.md` / `done.md`
71	are append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
72	slots out of document order).
73	
74	## Markdown anchor links
75	
76	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
77	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
78	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
79	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
80	official spec for auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
81	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
82	
83	## Todo format
84	
85	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest, with
86	the long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
87	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
88	description with reference links to more detail.
89	
90	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
91	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending), and for `## Bugs` it's
92	just an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
93	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
94	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
95	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
96	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
97	
98	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
99	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
100	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
101	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
102	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
103	
104	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews, and `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
105	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
106	
107	Example shape:
108	
109	```
110	# Todo
111	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
112	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
113	
114	# Done
115	- **Fixed issue Z** [[2]],[[3]]
116	
117	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
118	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
119	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
120	```
121	
122	## Done entry form
123	
124	A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
125	title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:
126	
127	```
128	- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
129	  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
130	  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
131	```
132	
133	- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
134	  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
135	  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
136	  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
137	  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
138	- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
139	  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
140	  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
141	  line, trades one of those for the other. See
142	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
143	  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
144	- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
145	  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
146	- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
147	  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
148	- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
149	  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.
150	
151	## Retiring Done entries
152	
153	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
154	log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:
155	
156	- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
157	  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
158	  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
159	- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
160	  version-of-record.
161	- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
162	  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
163	  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
164	  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
165	  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).
166	
167	Migration mechanics:
168	
169	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
170	  number).
171	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
172	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
173	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
174	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
175	
176	## Chores conventions
177	
178	### Headings and entries that record a commit
179	
180	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
181	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
182	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
183	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
184	version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
185	are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
186	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
187	E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
188	`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the cycle title
189	(the chores header's bare form, not the suffixed closing commit's: see
190	[Cycle bookend titles](prose.md#cycle-bookend-titles)), and its shape is in
191	[Done entry form](#done-entry-form).
192	
193	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
194	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
195	whatever fits. A `Ladder details` rung subsection is the exception among subsections: it is
196	commit-recording, its heading the rung's exact title. Among the commit-recording ones, exact
197	match is the strong default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a
198	record up with its commit.
199	
200	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
201	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
202	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
203	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
204	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
205	
206	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
207	free-form text. The convention applies going forward.
208	
209	### Chores section content: no edit list, git is the record
210	
211	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
212	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
213	design subsections, the moved block's `Ladder details` area among them (its subsections are
214	rung-titled and commit-recording, unlike the free-named design ones). Bullets here are
215	**conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
216	changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
217	body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
218	source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others, and none
219	restates another.
220	
221	The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
222	`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
223	narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
224	than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
225	[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
226	two don't drift.
227	
228	**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
229	chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
230	drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.
231	
232	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
233	Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
234	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
235	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
236	direction).
237	
238	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
239	places, and detail written twice drifts. The division:
240	
241	- git owns the mechanical record
242	- the body owns the problem and the solution
243	- chores owns the narrative
244	- the ladder's commit refs link them
245	
246	### Chores commit references
247	
248	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
249	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
250	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit. A single-commit cycle is a
251	one-rung ladder whose one step is the close-out:
252	
253	```
254	## refactor: extract config loader
255	
256	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 [refactor: split loader from parser][4]
257	- [[N]] refactor: extract config loader
258	
259	<intro paragraph...>
260	```
261	
262	- The rung form is `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
263	  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] [<title>][M]` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. `[M]` is the
264	  rung's subsection link, a file-local slot defined as a same-file fragment (`[M]: #<slug>`): it
265	  rides in from the working ladder and stays valid, since the subsections move into the same
266	  file, renumbered like any other slot, the closing rung's among them. No step number and no
267	  `(current)` / `(done)` marker, since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in
268	  `TODO.md > ## In Progress`). Landing order is the list order. See
269	  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
270	- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
271	  (see
272	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
273	  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
274	  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
275	  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
276	  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
277	  falsify.
278	- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
279	  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
280	  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
281	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
282	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
283	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
284	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
285	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`. The inner `[3]`
286	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
287	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
288	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
289	
290	```
291	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
292	```
293	
294	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
295	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
296	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
297	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
298	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
299	
300	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
301	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
302	is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung
303	opens with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version, and each push backfills the rungs of
304	the commits the previous push made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
305	lands. The commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See
306	cycle-protocol [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
307	
308	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines. The ladder form applies
309	going forward.
310	
311	### Chores file Table of Contents
312	
313	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
314	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
315	section, in file order.
316	
317	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
318	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
319	- The entry is appended by the close-out move that creates the section, and the entry text
320	  participates in the same last-edit title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
321	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
322	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.
323

description with reference links to more detail.

`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending), and for `## Bugs` it's
just an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.

Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.

`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews, and `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.

Example shape:

```
# Todo
1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
2. Fix bug Y [[1]]

# Done
- **Fixed issue Z** [[2]],[[3]]

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
[2]: issues.md#issue-z
[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
```

## Done entry form

A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:

```
- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
```

- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
  line, trades one of those for the other. See
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.

## Retiring Done entries

`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:

- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
  version-of-record.
- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).

Migration mechanics:

- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
  number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the cycle title
(the chores header's bare form, not the suffixed closing commit's: see
[Cycle bookend titles](prose.md#cycle-bookend-titles)), and its shape is in
[Done entry form](#done-entry-form).

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
whatever fits. A `Ladder details` rung subsection is the exception among subsections: it is
commit-recording, its heading the rung's exact title. Among the commit-recording ones, exact
match is the strong default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a
record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
free-form text. The convention applies going forward.

### Chores section content: no edit list, git is the record

A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
design subsections, the moved block's `Ladder details` area among them (its subsections are
rung-titled and commit-recording, unlike the free-named design ones). Bullets here are
**conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others, and none
restates another.

The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
two don't drift.

**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. The division:

- git owns the mechanical record
- the body owns the problem and the solution
- chores owns the narrative
- the ladder's commit refs link them

### Chores commit references

The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit. A single-commit cycle is a
one-rung ladder whose one step is the close-out:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 [refactor: split loader from parser][4]
- [[N]] refactor: extract config loader

<intro paragraph...>
```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] [<title>][M]` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. `[M]` is the
  rung's subsection link, a file-local slot defined as a same-file fragment (`[M]: #<slug>`): it
  rides in from the working ladder and stays valid, since the subsections move into the same
  file, renumbered like any other slot, the closing rung's among them. No step number and no
  `(current)` / `(done)` marker, since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in
  `TODO.md > ## In Progress`). Landing order is the list order. See
  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
  (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
  falsify.
- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`. The inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung
opens with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version, and each push backfills the rungs of
the commits the previous push made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
lands. The commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See
cycle-protocol [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines. The ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- The entry is appended by the close-out move that creates the section, and the entry text
  participates in the same last-edit title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

# Todo Backlog

This file uses [Prose form](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form). It holds lower-priority
`## Todo` entries, the long tail. When an entry becomes a priority, move it (and any refs it
cites) into `../TODO.md > ## Todo` at its priority rank (the list is strict-ranked, #1 highest),
then `fix-todo` to renumber.

Same formatting rules as `../TODO.md > ## Todo`. See
[Todo format](../agent-data/notes.md#todo-format). Run
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/todo-backlog.md` to renumber.

## Todo

1. Decide the three parked bookmarks that still hold unlanded work: `web-claude-tweaks`,
   `measure-reproducibility` and `ffq-spsc-notes`
   - measured 2026-08-13, `main..<bookmark>` per bookmark: `web-claude-tweaks` holds one commit
     (band-table bug fixes and bucket `debug_assert!()`s, 2026-07-24), `measure-reproducibility`
     three (a cycle opened and abandoned mid-ladder, 2026-08-04), `ffq-spsc-notes` one (an SPSC
     Q&A archive, 2026-07-28)
   - so each is land, rework, or discard, and only their owner can say which. The names are all
     that keep those commits reachable
   - `punctuation-sweep` and `fix-calibration` were swept on 2026-08-13, both fully merged into
     `main` with nothing unreachable. `punctuation-sweep` was local-only, never having reached
     `origin`
   - the deletions publish in one push, `jj git push` naming each with a repeated `-b`
     ([chores-07](chores/chores-07.md#landing-measured))
2. Policy pins, parameters stay: move the rules living in `custom*` into the pinned agent-files,
   leaving the layer holding only declared values (raised 2026-08-16, wink review pending, then
   express our opinion to vc-x1)
   - the test for any line in `custom*`: would a diff between two members be a *disagreement*
     (policy, belongs pinned, where the diff is a reviewable proposal) or an *identity* (a name,
     a path, a command string, a width)? Only the second belongs in the layer
   - wants one new pinned convention, stated once: a pinned rule may reference a parameter the
     project layer declares, and an undeclared parameter leaves the rule inert, the same shape
     as versioning.md's medium conditionals
   - the migration it licenses: the Messaging policy moves pinned, parameterized by the messages
     repo path and the member name, which dissolves the 2026-08-07 dead-text objection that
     moved it out of `AGENTS.md`. Membership stays parameters (parked awaiting `vc-x1 config`
     keys), and the dogfood log is a per-member record, out of pinned regardless, `notes/` its
     natural long-term home
   - validation already models the split: the pinned checklists own the slots and the
     exit-status rule, `custom-family.md` fills the slots with this project's commands
   - the same schema/instance shape as vc-x1's `vc-config.md` against `.vc-config.md`, proposed
     for the instruction set itself
   - a reversal of a rule vc-x1 took from our 2026-08-07 proposal, so the message to them argues
     the reversal, not just the convention

```
feat: write a per-run JSON record

The report prints and is gone: no run's numbers survive the session
that produced them, so comparing two runs means comparing a terminal
scrollback against a memory. A record is a machine-readable summary of
one bench result, written beside the unchanged display rather than
instead of it.

* nothing a run measured could be re-analysed after the fact
  - --record <path> appends one NDJSON object per bench result: a
    fixed quantile ladder, the block-mean series, whole-histogram
    stats, and the warm verdict with its settle time and clock
* an archived number is ambiguous without its machine state
  - every record carries the power policy including the frequency
    clamps and boost, the host, the pin pool, and verbatim --tag
    pairs, so a policy delta can no longer masquerade as a code delta
  - the delivered clock is now sampled at every batch seam and rides
    the record, so the series spans the bench instead of stopping at
    warmup's end, and a pinned run's collapse to min = max will be the
    pin's own verification
* a record outlives the binary that wrote it
  - schema_version stamps the layout, the describe-record command
    prints the field dictionary, and a test fails on any record key
    the dictionary misses or names in vain
* a rerun must not destroy earlier evidence
  - a directory path writes one file per run stamped with time, host,
    and bench, a file path appends, the open never truncates, and a
    failed write dies loudly rather than losing the run silently

No bug — the two numbers are from **two different runs**, and each run is internally consistent:

- The output you pasted is a plain `iiac-perf min-now` (no `--record`): `outer=8,322,999`, and 8,322,999 / 65,536 samples-per-batch = 127 batches.
- `tmp/xx.toml` came from your earlier `--record` run: it carries `samples=7,891,112`, and 7,891,112 / 65,536 = 120 full batches + 1 partial = **121** batches — exactly matching its 121 `clock_t_s` entries, one per seam, none missed. I also checked the gaps: the sample spacing is a uniform ~41 ms with no holes, covering the run end to end.

Batch counts vary run to run (across 13 runs just now I saw 116 to 132), because a batch is "65,536 samples" and the sample rate wanders with the clock. In all 13 runs `clock_t_s` length equaled the batch count exactly. A shortfall *is* possible by design — a failed clock read is skipped rather than faked, which is why each sample carries its own timestamp — but none occurred here.

On "all of the other arrays are much shorter": that's by design, nothing scales with batches except the three clock arrays. `quantile_pcts`/`quantile_ns` are the fixed 13-rung ladder, and `block_*` are null because the run had no `--blocks`. Per-batch summaries are deliberately not recorded — the record carries the block-mean series for replication and the seam clock for the machine, while the batch series stays the display grade's grain.

One improvement this surfaced: the record doesn't carry its own batch count, so the cross-check you tried required deriving it from `samples`. I could add a `batches` field (one more documented key, trivially cheap). Want it in this rung?

content.text:
Two separate answers:

**Why is the clock the only per-batch data?** First, a small correction: it's three numbers per seam, not one — `clock_t_s` (when), `clock_cpu` (where), `clock_khz` (the reading) are parallel arrays. But your broader observation is right: the harness *has* a rich per-batch summary internally (robust floor, mean, max, sample count, census of over-floor samples — the time series the grade block reads), and none of it goes in the record. That was the rung's spec as laddered: the record answers two questions, "what was the machine doing" (policy + seam clock) and "how repeatable is the number" (block-mean series, quantile ladder), and the per-batch workload series stayed display-side. The clock series itself only joined the record by your call on 2026-08-16, for pin verification. Recording the full batch summaries is a legitimate future want — cheap to add behind a `schema_version` bump if a re-analysis ever needs the within-run workload timeline — but I'd keep it out of this rung rather than grow the scope mid-review.

**Should the timestamp be an integer instead of f64?** I'd argue the float is right here, for consistency rather than economy:

- Every time-valued field in the record is seconds as a JSON number: `duration_s`, `settle_s`, `warm_used_s`, `suspended_s`. Making just the clock timestamps integer milliseconds or nanoseconds would put two time units in one record.
- The value is seconds *from warmup start* on the same axis the report prints (`step @2.35s`), so a reader can line a record up with a saved report without conversion.
- Precision is not actually at risk: an f64 holds ~15-16 significant digits, so at run scale (seconds to hours) it is exact to well under a microsecond, against a seam cadence of ~40 ms. And JSON has no integer type anyway — most consumers (jq included) parse every number as a double, so a u64 nanosecond count above 2^53 would be the representation that *loses* digits in practice.

So: sub-second timestamps as float seconds is the deliberate, uniform choice, and u64 would buy exactness the consumer side would immediately throw away.

The plain version: the file actually stores three values per batch pause — the time, which CPU, and the speed. The richer per-batch statistics exist in the program but were left out of the file on purpose, and could be added later without breaking old files. The time is stored as a decimal number of seconds because every other time in the file is too, and at these sizes decimals are exact far beyond what's needed — while big whole-number timestamps are the thing JSON tools actually mangle.

The raw number the harness actually reads is an integer nanosecond count from the run's origin, and with the run data in the record anything else (seconds, wall-clock) is calculable. And even your 2^53 exposure never bites: a 10-hour run is ~3.6e13 ns, well inside exact-double range.

I'll change the series to `clock_t_ns` (u64, ns from warmup start), keeping derived scalar summaries (`duration_s` and friends) as they are — raw series, derived scalars. Let me look at the exact current code:

content.text:
```
feat: write a per-run JSON record

Running iiac-perf leaves no permanent record of a run: the report
prints to the terminal and is not durable. This change adds that
capability. A record is a machine-readable summary of one bench
result, written beside the unchanged display rather than instead of
it.

* nothing a run measured could be re-analysed after the fact
  - --record <path> appends one NDJSON object per bench result: a
    fixed quantile ladder, the block-mean series, whole-histogram
    stats, and the warm verdict with its settle time and clock
* an archived number is ambiguous without its machine state
  - every record carries the power policy including the frequency
    clamps and boost, the host, the pin pool, and verbatim --tag
    pairs, so a policy delta can no longer masquerade as a code delta
  - the delivered clock is now sampled at every batch seam and rides
    the record, so the series spans the bench instead of stopping at
    warmup's end, and a pinned run's collapse to min = max will be the
    pin's own verification
* a record outlives the binary that wrote it
  - schema_version stamps the layout, the describe-record command
    prints the field dictionary, and a test fails on any record key
    the dictionary misses or names in vain
* a rerun must not destroy earlier evidence
  - a directory path writes one file per run stamped with time, host,
    and bench, a file path appends, the open never truncates, and a
    failed write dies loudly rather than losing the run silently
```

Also still open: the `batches` count field — add it, or leave it derivable from `samples`? Stopped for your review.
